---
title: "Verification Bandwidth, Claim Ledgers, and Proof"
unit_id: "unit-15"
---

## The Claim Everyone Approved

The release note now uses a coherent, current context. It says that controller
version 8 completed a bounded gantry trial, the run stopped after oscillation,
the observed trace is linked through an approved public summary, and the
claim-bearing safety campaign has not run.

Five reviewers inspect it. The schema checker confirms the record shape. The
link checker confirms that every public URL resolves. A Lean theorem confirms
that the authored stop lease cannot remain active after its recorded expiry.
A model reviewer finds no unsupported sentence in the note it sees. A human
reviewer checks the prose and approves publication.

The claim still has a defect. The public summary omits that one sensor stream
was unavailable during the final interval. The schema did not require that
field. The link checker could not infer it. The Lean theorem was about lease
state, not sensor coverage. The model reviewer received only the release note
and summary. The human spent four minutes and assumed the technical checks had
covered the evidence.

Every reviewer performed its assigned work. The joined verification program
was inadequate.

This failure is not solved by adding one more approval label. It requires a
claim identity that survives wording changes, an explicit set of obligations,
enough verification capacity to discharge them, artifacts that state what they
actually check, objections and defeaters that remain attached, a bounded
support decision, and a repair path to every known consumer.

Verification Bandwidth asks whether the system had enough appropriate checking
capacity for this claim. Claim Ledgers preserve what the system currently
believes and why. Proof-Carrying Claims bind selected propositions to formal,
executable, empirical, source, or adversarial artifacts. Executable
specifications and Lean prove narrow properties under explicit assumptions.
Proof-carrying contracts let those facts travel without broadening. None of
these owners is a truth machine. Together, they make a claim challengeable and
correctable.

## Verification Starts With Obligations

A verification program begins by asking what could make a claim wrong or
misleading for its intended consumer. It does not begin with whichever checker
is convenient.

The release-note claim has several obligations. Identity requires that the
controller, software, configuration, trial, and evidence refer to the same
run. Observation requires that the stop and oscillation statements match the
recorded sensors and their missingness. Scope requires that a bounded trial not
become a deployment claim. Authority requires that the evidence and wording be
permitted for the public consumer. Formal structure requires that any stated
lease or lifecycle property match its encoded model. Publication requires that
links, accessibility, and release state be current. Residual custody requires
that unavailable sensors and unexecuted campaigns remain visible.

Each obligation names a mode of failure, required context, checking method,
competence assumptions, independence needs, cost, deadline, and consequence if
unresolved. Some can be discharged by deterministic code. Some require source
inspection, formal proof, empirical measurement, adversarial review, domain
expertise, affected-party input, or continued abstention.

The obligation set is itself defeasible. Reviewers can miss a dimension. A
well-formed list does not prove completeness. The system therefore records who
constructed it, which threat model and consumer informed it, which templates or
prior incidents were consulted, and which unknowns remain.

This prevents tool-driven verification. A team with a theorem prover should
not turn every question into a theorem. A team with model judges should not
reduce every question to prose scoring. The claim determines the obligations;
the obligations select the routes.

## Verification Bandwidth Is Qualified Capacity

Verification bandwidth is not the number of tokens spent criticizing an
answer. It is the claim-specific capacity to perform the checks that matter
before the decision deadline.

A verifier has a mode, scope, competence envelope, context requirement,
throughput, latency, cost, error profile, dependence graph, and authority. A
static analyzer may check one program property quickly. A domain expert may
identify a missing premise that no local test encodes. A model reviewer may
screen many claims while sharing failure modes with the generator. A formal
kernel may check a proof exactly while saying nothing about whether the theorem
matches the world.

The allocation problem is bipartite. One side contains claim obligations. The
other contains available checks and reviewers. An edge says that a verifier is
qualified to address an obligation under specified context and assumptions.
The system must choose enough edges to cover the required obligations within
time and resource limits.

Coverage is not merely a count. Twelve checkers may all inspect grammar while
no one inspects sensor missingness. Two apparently independent model judges may
share training data, provider infrastructure, prompt framing, or evidence. A
human approval after reading only a summary cannot cover a source-level
obligation.

The result can be adequate, narrowed, escalated, abstained, blocked, disputed,
or expired. Adequacy means the declared required checks were competently
performed for this claim and consumer. It does not mean the claim is true.
Narrowing changes the claim to fit what can be checked. Blocking preserves the
unresolved obligations rather than replacing them with reviewer confidence.

## Verification Is a Portfolio Decision

No serious system can verify every claim with every available method. Human
attention, model calls, proof engineering, experiments, source access, and
decision time are finite. Verification therefore needs an allocation policy,
not an aspiration to check everything.

The policy begins with consequence, uncertainty, reversibility, affected
parties, consumer count, propagation depth, novelty, adversarial exposure, and
deadline. A low-consequence sentence in an internal draft may need citation
lint and a visible uncertainty marker. A claim that controls deployment,
rights, money, physical action, or recursive improvement deserves a broader
and more independent program.

Expected information value helps choose the next check. If two observations
would lead to the same decision, the cheaper one may suffice. If one missing
sensor stream could reverse the verdict, inspecting that stream outranks
another general prose review. If the decision can safely wait, acquiring fresh
evidence may dominate argument. If delay itself causes harm, the system may
choose a narrower reversible action with monitoring instead of pretending to
finish verification.

The allocation record names candidate checks, predicted decision impact,
cost, latency, dependence, failure risk, chosen sequence, rejected routes, and
stop conditions. Prediction errors remain visible. A check expected to be
decisive may return unknown; a cheap source lookup may uncover the core defect.
The system learns allocation policy only from outcomes that retain the full
denominator.

Parallel checks can reduce latency but may waste resources or contaminate
independence. A reviewer who sees another verdict can anchor on it. A model
judge asked after a human decision may reproduce the decision rather than
provide a distinct failure path. The plan states which checks are blind,
sequential, shared-context, or contingent.

Verification also needs stopping rules. Stop when required obligations are
covered to the declared standard, when a material unresolved obligation forces
block or narrowing, when expected information value falls below cost, when the
deadline requires a safe fallback, or when the review cycle reaches its cap.
“Keep reviewing until approval” is not a stopping rule.

Budgets cannot become permission to ignore rights or severe hazards. Some
obligations are hard constraints. If they cannot be checked, the action narrows
or stops. The portfolio policy optimizes among admissible programs; it does not
price away boundaries it lacks authority to trade.

This allocation layer gives verification bandwidth an operational meaning. It
can be evaluated against fixed checklists, uniform review, expert-only review,
model-only review, and ordinary risk-based practice. Success means better
decisions and correction under the same complete budget, not more elaborate
packets.

## Context Adequacy Is Claim-Relative

The previous unit built coherent context transactions. Coherence is necessary
but not enough. A context can be internally consistent and still omit what a
verifier needs.

Context adequacy begins with the claim, obligation, verifier, and decision. The
link checker needs the rendered public URLs. The observation reviewer needs
the trace, sensor inventory, calibration and missingness, trial configuration,
and exact claim. The Lean kernel needs theorem source, imported definitions,
and compiler environment. The public reviewer needs intelligible evidence and
known limitations.

The adequacy record names requested objects, mounted objects, denied or absent
objects, transformations, resolution quality, freshness, contradictions,
truncation, verifier use, and residual effect. A large context window can be
inadequate if the decisive sensor metadata is missing. A small exact packet can
be adequate for a narrow hash check.

More context can reduce verification bandwidth. Distractors consume attention,
hide decisive evidence, and increase the chance that a model or human accepts
a plausible but irrelevant argument. Compression can help if it preserves the
obligation-specific facts and rescue path. It harms when it removes the very
missingness or dissent that should change the verdict.

The verifier should attest to what it actually used, not merely what was
available in the mount. A citation may be present but unread. A test result may
be visible but misunderstood. A model context may include the policy while the
generated answer ignores it. Use evidence remains fallible, but it narrows the
gap between context delivery and verification work.

## A Claim Needs an Identity Before a Score

Claims change wording, location, support, scope, and consumers over time. A
stable claim identity lets the system track that history without pretending
that every wording is equivalent.

The release-note claim can be represented as a structured proposition: for
trial identity T, controller version V, configuration C, and interval I, the
observed run stopped after oscillation under evidence packet E. Its public
surface includes prose that renders that proposition. A separate non-claim
states that the record does not establish deployment safety.

The claim record binds identity, current wording, semantic representation,
scope, time, affected parties, consumer, support state, evidence and source
refs, proof and test refs, objections, defeaters, dependencies, authority,
maximum inference, residuals, and surface locations. The identity does not
guarantee that the representation is correct. It makes disagreement and repair
addressable.

Surface identity remains separate. The same claim may appear in a technical
chapter, Human Reader chapter, release note, diagram, status panel, API, and
model memory. Each surface can drift. The claim ledger records which version
each surface presented and which consumers acknowledged a change.

A new wording that changes quantifier, population, time, modality, causal
force, or support boundary creates a proposed claim revision, not a cosmetic
edit. A faithful paraphrase may retain the claim identity with a mapping
receipt. Ambiguous changes route to review.

## The Ledger Is Append-Only Belief History

A claim ledger records events rather than overwriting the current label. Events
include proposal, source attachment, evidence admission, objection, proof
result, test result, contradiction, narrowing, promotion, demotion, refutation,
deprecation, supersession, consumer use, and surface repair.

Each event binds the previous claim version, proposed next version, actor or
process, authority, evidence, verifier, time, affected obligations, support
effect, consumer effect, and residuals. Rejected proposals remain in history.
A later reader can reconstruct why the current state exists and which
alternative was declined.

Append-only does not mean immutable error. A false claim can be demoted or
refuted. Its historical events remain so the system can find decisions made
under it. Deleting the record would make correction harder and permit the same
claim to re-enter without its defeaters.

Concurrency matters. Two reviewers may propose incompatible revisions from
the same base. The ledger should not silently make the last write win. It
records the branch, detects the stale base, and requires a merge or adjudication
event. Consumers continue using the last accepted version or enter safe hold
according to consequence.

The ledger does not own the support decision simply because it stores it.
Evidence and governance policies determine who may change support. The ledger
checks that the requested transition is authorized and complete, then records
the result exactly.

## Evidence Events Do Not Promote Themselves

A passing test, theorem, source, benchmark, review, or runtime observation is
an evidence artifact. It does not automatically move the parent claim.

The transition proposal identifies the claim, current support, requested next
state, exact artifact, relevance, quality dimensions, scope, counterevidence,
alternative explanations, competence, independence, reproduction, consumer
consequence, and maximum inference. An authorized policy evaluates that
packet. The outcome may promote, narrow, demote, refute, preserve, or defer.

This separation prevents self-promotion. A benchmark runner cannot decide that
its own result proves the architecture. A proof producer cannot generalize its
theorem. A chapter author cannot convert source synthesis into external
validation by changing a label. The artifact can propose; a distinct gate
decides.

Negative results need the same care. An instrument failure does not refute the
idea. A competent null result may narrow a mechanism. An adversarial failure
may block a route without proving every related system unsafe. The ledger keeps
test competence, result direction, inference boundary, and parent support
separate.

In the release-note case, discovering the missing sensor stream should at
least narrow the public observation claim or add an explicit residual. Whether
it demotes a broader controller claim depends on the broader claim's identity
and evidence, not on textual proximity.

## Defeaters and Maximum Inference Travel With the Claim

A **defeater** states what would weaken, block, or reverse the claim. It may be
an observed contradiction, missing premise, failed replication, expired
policy, changed implementation, unqualified evaluator, alternative causal
explanation, or unresolved affected-party concern.

Defeaters are not footnotes. They participate in admission and consumer
decisions. A claim with an active material defeater may remain visible for
research while being blocked from planning or publication. Resolving a
defeater requires an artifact and authority appropriate to its type.

**Maximum inference** states the strongest conclusion the current packet can
support. For the release note, it might permit: “This exact recorded run stopped
after the observed oscillation under incomplete final-interval sensing.” It
forbids conclusions about controller detection competence, causal attribution,
general reliability, or deployment safety.

The boundary should be machine-visible and human-readable. Downstream systems
can compare a proposed use with permitted inference. Readers can see why a
claim is narrow without parsing an internal ledger.

Maximum inference can contract when evidence is invalidated and expand only
through an authorized transition. It does not expand because a sentence is
repeated across many surfaces.

## Formality Has Several Lanes

“Verified” is too ambiguous for consequential claims. The architecture names
the artifact lane.

A **schema** checks shape, required fields, enums, and local consistency. A
**deterministic validator** checks an executable rule over artifacts. A
**unit or integration test** checks selected behavior in an implementation. A
**benchmark** measures outcomes under a protocol. A **formal proof** establishes
a proposition in a logic from definitions and assumptions. A **runtime
observation** records what happened in an environment. A **source review**
checks a relation to external literature or records. A **human or adversarial
review** supplies bounded judgment and challenge.

These lanes can reinforce one another. They cannot substitute without an
explicit bridge. A schema-valid trace can contain false values. A theorem about
an abstract state machine can fail to describe the code. Passing code tests do
not prove all inputs. A benchmark can be contaminated. A runtime observation
can be mismeasured. A human can misunderstand the dossier.

The proof envelope maps a prose claim to the appropriate artifacts and records
what remains outside each. Some claims should stay as research questions until
an operational predicate can be stated honestly.

## Executable Specifications Make Disagreement Concrete

An executable specification turns selected meanings into states, transitions,
preconditions, postconditions, and invariants. It is valuable when a disputed
boundary can be stated precisely enough to reject a bad case.

For the release note, an executable record might require exact trial identity,
current public evidence, explicit sensor coverage, active policy, nonexpired
lease, unchanged support state, and no deployment inference. A validator can
reject a packet that omits sensor missingness or references the stale summary.

The specification is not the world. It can encode the wrong obligation, omit a
stakeholder, or simplify time and uncertainty. Its provenance should identify
which prose claim, incident, policy, or design decision produced each predicate.
Counterexamples and rejected fixtures help reviewers see the intended boundary.

Specifications should be small enough to understand and connected to a real
consumer. Proving hundreds of projections over unused records creates formal
surface area without reducing uncertainty. The preferred target is a
load-bearing transition, impossibility, conservation rule, noninterference
property, or consumer gate.

## Lean Proves the Encoded Proposition

Lean can check that a theorem follows from authored definitions and premises.
That is a powerful and deliberately narrow fact.

A theorem may prove that an expired lease cannot authorize a transition, that
a rejected event preserves state, that accepted runs retain identity, that
support is not assigned by a transaction, or that two thin summaries cannot
determine a richer state. These results remove ambiguity from the modeled
record system.

They do not prove that the environment supplied truthful fields, the code
refines the model, the policy is legitimate, the theorem captures the reader's
intended claim, or the system is safe. Those require additional bridges.

The proof packet binds theorem ID, source digest, definitions, assumptions,
Lean and dependency versions, build command, checked result, interpretation
mapping, implementation binding, consumer, expiry, non-claims, and residuals.
A changed definition, source, compiler, or consumer can invalidate the packet
without making the historical theorem false.

Neural-network verification has the same boundary. A verifier may establish a
property for one checkpoint, preprocessing pipeline, input region, arithmetic
semantics, and output predicate. It does not establish natural-distribution
robustness, model intent, privacy, or whole-agent safety.

## Proof and Use Answer Different Questions

Suppose a system discovers a reusable sorting routine and proves it correct.
That settles an important question about the routine's semantics. It does not
show that the compiler emitted the code described by the proof, or that adding
the routine to a search library helps solve future problems under a fixed
budget.

Those are three claims: the abstraction is valid, the executed artifact
preserves it, and its availability improves later outcomes. Each needs its own
receipt. A verified routine can be too expensive to retrieve, redundant with
the baseline, or harmful because it enlarges the search vocabulary. Conversely,
a useful heuristic can improve outcomes without carrying a theorem.

Formal methods are strongest when they keep these boundaries visible. The
proof does not become weaker because it declines to certify transfer. It
becomes more trustworthy because readers can see exactly where semantic
certainty ends and experimental evidence must begin.

## Proof-Carrying Claims Bind Interpretation

A proof-carrying claim packages a proposition with the artifact that supports
one of its boundaries. The package includes the claim identity and version,
formal or executable target, interpretation mapping, verifier, artifact,
failed attempts, support effect, consumer, expiry, dissent, and non-claims.

Interpretation mapping is essential. A perfectly valid theorem about
`leaseActive = false` may not establish that the physical controller stopped.
The package says which natural-language phrase corresponds to which predicate
and what bridge remains empirical.

Not every claim needs formal proof. A citation dossier, executable procedure,
reproducible experiment, adversarial case, or structured human review may be
the correct justification. “Proof-carrying” names the discipline of carrying
the exact justification and boundary, not a promise that all knowledge reduces
to theorem proving.

The package can fail. The theorem may not resolve. The interpretation may be
ambiguous. The artifact may be stale. The verifier may be unsupported. A
failed attempt remains in the denominator and routes to repair, narrowing, or
continued block.

## Proof Contracts Travel Without Promotion

Proof-carrying contracts let finite structural facts move between producers
and consumers. A contract can bind theorem IDs, fingerprints, receipt state,
proof boundary, source refs, consumer state, staleness policy, support effect,
and non-claims.

The useful property is transport discipline. A planner can consume a proven
finite ordering predicate without inferring that the plan is useful. A memory
service can consume a revocation invariant without inferring that every copy
was found. A routing service can consume a structural tensor property without
inferring model-quality advantage.

Circle Calculus supplies one source family and external receipt lineage for
this idea. The ASI Stack's local consumer can check pinned receipt boundaries,
mutations, and finite lifecycle properties. That does not mean this repository
built the external calculus, resolved every theorem from source, or validated
downstream model behavior.

A proof receipt should make overclaiming harder. If a consumer can drop the
non-claims or reuse the receipt after its source or implementation changes, the
transport failed even if the original proof was valid.

## Adversarial Review Is a Bounded Tribunal

Some claims remain consequential and interpretation-heavy after formal and
empirical work. They need structured challenge.

A tribunal packet binds the case, claim version, evidence, proof and test
artifacts, affected parties, reviewer roles, dependence graph, attack plan,
findings, dissent, unresolved questions, cycle cap, verdict, appeal, required
actions, and writeback request.

Reviewer diversity is functional, not demographic bookkeeping alone. One
reviewer may attack source validity, another formal interpretation, another
runtime correspondence, another rights or public consequence. Shared model,
organization, incentives, evidence, or infrastructure can make several
reviewers one failure path.

The tribunal can approve narrowly, require revision, block, dispute, or return
unknown. It does not create truth by vote. A complete dossier can lead to a
wrong verdict, and a correct verdict can be generalized beyond its case.

Appeal requires new evidence, identified error, changed policy, or another
declared basis. Repeating the same prompt until a favorable judge appears is
not appeal. Cycle caps prevent unlimited review from consuming the whole
system.

## Disagreement Is an Output, Not a Defect

Review systems often pressure several judgments into one scalar verdict. That
can erase the exact disagreement that a decision-maker needs.

One reviewer may accept the claim's observational wording but reject its
sensor coverage. Another may accept the evidence and dispute public authority.
A formal reviewer may confirm the lease theorem while objecting that its
interpretation map is incomplete. These are not three noisy estimates of one
probability. They concern different obligations.

The verdict packet preserves each finding, evidence basis, scope, dependence,
confidence or uncertainty representation, requested action, and unresolved
response. It records where reviewers agree, where their methods share a root,
and which disagreements can change the consumer decision. An aggregate can be
computed for a policy that genuinely needs one, but the underlying structure
remains available.

Some disputes can be resolved by a new observation or proof. Others concern
values, jurisdiction, acceptable risk, or ontology and require an authorized
decision rather than more evidence. The ledger must not describe a governance
choice as though a fact checker settled it.

Minority findings gain neither automatic correctness nor automatic dismissal.
A dissent can block if policy assigns it that power for a specified hazard; it
can trigger another check; it can remain attached as a residual; or it can be
overruled through a recorded authority path. The disposition and rationale
travel with the accepted claim.

Preserved disagreement improves future correction. If the missing sensor
stream later proves decisive, the system can identify which reviewer raised
the issue, which evidence was unavailable, why the concern did or did not
block, and which consumers relied on the resulting verdict. A single approval
score would have destroyed that learning signal.

## Runtime Truth Is a Separate Bridge

The formal model may say that a stop transition disables authority. The code
may pass tests showing that it emits the stop command. The runtime trace may
show the command was sent. The plant may nevertheless continue moving because
the actuator failed.

Each crossing needs evidence: specification to theorem, theorem to code, code
to deployed artifact, artifact to execution, execution to observation, and
observation to claim. A break at one crossing does not invalidate every fact
above it, but it blocks the broader conclusion.

Implementation refinement can use proof, testing, model checking, trace
comparison, code generation, or restricted trusted components. Runtime
correspondence needs exact build identity, configuration, environment,
instrumentation, time, and independent-enough effect observation.

The release-note claim is observational. The Lean lease theorem is relevant to
the control record, but it cannot fill the missing sensor interval. The claim
must retain that residual unless another admissible observation closes it.

## Downgrades Must Reach Every Known Consumer

Correction fails when the central ledger changes but downstream surfaces keep
the old claim.

A downgrade event computes the known dependency closure: plans, memory
objects, reports, pages, diagrams, APIs, benchmarks, policies, training data,
and external releases that consumed the affected version. Each consumer has a
repair policy: invalidate, rebuild, annotate, quarantine, notify, appeal, or
record irreversible residual.

The ledger tracks proposed scope and observed mutations. A surface can
acknowledge the new claim, dispute applicability, or remain unreachable. The
central transition is not complete simply because one database row changed.

For the release note, the missing sensor stream may require revised wording in
the technical chapter, public summary, release note, memory object, and future
prompt context. An already copied external post may be irrecoverable. The
residual stays attached to the claim and release history.

Unknown consumers remain a real limitation. Exact lineage covers only recorded
uses. Search, telemetry, access logs, and repository scans can discover more,
but no clean local closure proves universal propagation.

Known consumers return acknowledgments bound to the changed claim version.
They record whether they rebuilt, narrowed, quarantined, annotated, appealed,
or could not repair; which artifact now replaces the old basis; and which
effects remain irreversible. Silence after notification is not counted as
successful repair. Consequential consumers enter safe hold when their policy
requires acknowledgment before reuse.

## Failure Cases

**Obligation omission.** Every assigned check passes because the decisive
failure mode was never listed.

**Verifier monoculture.** Several reviewers share one model, source, prompt, or
institutional incentive.

**Context abundance.** Large packets hide the decisive evidence and exhaust
attention.

**Context nonuse.** Required evidence is mounted but never inspected.

**Claim alias drift.** Different surfaces appear to discuss one claim while
their quantifiers or scope diverge.

**Last-write-wins belief.** Concurrent revisions erase disagreement and stale
base versions.

**Evidence self-promotion.** A producer upgrades the parent claim from its own
artifact.

**Negative-result overreach.** An inadequate instrument is treated as a
mechanism refutation.

**Proof substitution.** A theorem about records is presented as environmental
or deployment truth.

**Implementation gap.** Proven definitions do not match the code or deployed
configuration.

**Receipt laundering.** A downstream consumer drops the proof boundary,
expiry, or non-claims.

**Tribunal theater.** Reviewers fill every field without possessing the context
or competence to challenge the claim.

**Review exhaustion.** Low-value checks consume scarce human and computational
capacity while high-consequence obligations wait.

**Surface orphaning.** A downgrade reaches the ledger but not a report,
diagram, model memory, or release.

**Irreversible publication.** A corrected claim cannot retract copies already
distributed.

**Formal surface inflation.** Theorem and validator counts rise without
connecting to a live consumer or uncertainty.

## The Strongest Simpler Baseline

The strongest ordinary system uses version control, issue tracking, citations,
tests, code review, continuous integration, a database of claims, release
checklists, and human approval. It can provide excellent verification without
one universal ledger or proof-carrying protocol.

That baseline should remain preferred for many projects. The additional
architecture earns its cost where claims persist across many surfaces and
consumers; where support changes need exact authority and history; where formal,
empirical, source, runtime, and review artifacts must remain distinct; or where
downstream invalidation has material consequences.

The comparison should measure correction rate, false acceptance, false block,
calibration, time to find decisive evidence, proof-scope errors, downstream
repair, reviewer load, latency, compute, implementation complexity, and
residual harm. Metadata completeness is not the outcome.

A thin ledger plus excellent reviewers may outperform a rich protocol with
weak obligation discovery. A small set of focused tests may beat a large
formalization program. The architecture should consolidate wherever ordinary
records produce equal correction and scope discipline at lower total cost.

## What the Current Work Establishes

The five technical owners have distinct bounded artifacts. Their combination
does not create a stronger support state.

Verification Bandwidth has four implemented targets. Its authored evidence
includes three valid and five rejecting admission records, two valid and seven
rejecting contradiction traces, three valid and five rejecting capacity
traces, a twelve-unit record with 66 pairwise obligations of which 18 are
checked and 48 remain residual, and a 24-obligation decomposition with six
boundary checks. Its current 35-theorem replacement surface reaches evidence-
gate handoff and rejects 31 handoff mutations. A three-instrument sacrificial
campaign reached six-of-six eligibility accuracy and complete required-
residual recall but admitted only three of six extraction interfaces, so its
held-out workload stayed sealed.

Claim Ledgers has four implemented targets through 27 refinement declarations,
with sixteen weak declarations retired and four bounded legacy lemmas retained.
Five valid and seven rejecting revision fixtures plus one valid and eleven
rejecting historical lifecycle records feed five reachable stages, 22 route
cases, and 34 rejected lifecycle mutations.

Proof-Carrying Claims and Adversarial Review has five implemented targets and
44 live declarations across its retained and refinement modules. The proof-
carrying surface uses three valid and five rejecting fixtures, two valid and
seven rejecting dossier cases, six stages, 23 routes, and 36 rejected
mutations. The Tribunal surface uses three valid and five rejecting reviews,
one valid and eleven rejecting method or independence records, seven stages,
28 routes, and 45 rejected mutations.

Circle's current local surface contains 28 Lean declarations. Its public
records include two schema-valid fixtures, a pinned external receipt slice, a
consumer gate that accepts one receipt and rejects four mutations, and a
digest-verified archive of nine contracts and four policy receipts with five
rejected controls. The lifecycle checks 45 reachable states through 360
transitions, nine revoked-lineage states through 72 contained transitions,
eight trace splits, 16 lifecycle mutations, and 15 semantic mutations. A
narrow non-core receipt transition does not promote the chapter core.

The Executable Specifications proof envelope has two implemented targets and a
28-declaration local module. Its independent audit executes a ten-event
authority-lease trace, checks eleven composition splits, rejects 33 route
cases, exercises expiry and a thin-summary collision, and rejects 19 complete-
transport mutations.

All five cores remain `Design rationale` at `argument`. These results do not
establish obligation completeness, natural claim identity, source or artifact
truth, semantic equivalence, verifier soundness, reviewer competence or
independence in fact, verdict correctness, implementation refinement, runtime
correspondence, useful advantage, safety, deployment, reproduction, or
transfer.

## From a Minimum Ledger to an Evidence Fabric

A minimum implementation can use the release-note claim. Give it a stable
identity and exact public wording. Construct obligations for identity,
observation, missingness, scope, authority, formal lease state, publication,
and residuals. Allocate deterministic, source, formal, runtime, model, and
human checks under a fixed budget. Record which context each verifier requested
and used.

Bind the lease theorem to its interpretation and non-claims. Run an adversarial
review that specifically seeks obligation omission and shared reviewer
dependence. Submit the joined artifacts to a separate support gate. Inject the
missing sensor stream, require narrowing, and propagate the revision to every
known surface. Preserve one unreachable external copy as an irreversible
residual.

The next stage needs natural multi-surface claims with changing evidence,
concurrent revisions, ontology migration, stale proofs, implementation drift,
reviewer disagreement, and actual external effects. Compare ordinary issue
tracking, evidence databases, model review, expert review, tests, and formal
methods under matched information and cost. Measure correction and decision
quality, not packet completion.

The mature evidence fabric would allocate verification effort by consequence,
uncertainty, expected information value, reviewer dependence, and deadline. It
would connect sources, proofs, tests, runtime observations, objections,
affected-party input, support decisions, consumers, and repair without making
one evaluator sovereign.

Claims could be promoted, narrowed, demoted, refuted, or retired while their
history and downstream consequences remain recoverable. Proofs and receipts
would travel as bounded facts. Unknown and dispute would remain operational
states. Formal work would grow only where it removes a live ambiguity or
protects a real consumer.

## The Strongest Objection

Rich ledgers and proofs can preserve impeccable metadata around a false or
irrelevant conclusion. They can also consume the verification bandwidth they
are meant to manage. Reviewers may spend more time checking receipts than
examining the world.

The objection is correct. Traceability cannot rescue a bad ontology, omitted
obligation, weak evaluator, or irrelevant theorem. Formal precision can make a
mistake look authoritative. A complicated support workflow can discourage
small corrections and shift power toward whoever controls the ledger.

The architecture responds by treating obligation discovery, context use,
reviewer competence, outcome quality, and total burden as empirical questions.
It allows thin records, low-consequence fast paths, bounded review cycles, and
ordinary tools. It forbids theorem counts, packet completeness, or approval
counts from becoming outcome metrics.

The ledger should be judged by whether consequential errors are found earlier,
claims are scoped more accurately, corrections reach consumers, and residuals
remain visible at acceptable cost. If it does not improve those outcomes, it
should contract.

## Evidence That Would Change the Conclusion

Simpler evidence records that produce equal correction, calibration, proof-
scope discipline, consumer repair, and reviewer independence at lower total
cost would justify consolidation. Evidence that formal envelopes systematically
increase deference or hide semantic mismatch would narrow where they should be
used.

Support for the broader design would require prospective natural claim
campaigns with independent semantic and outcome labels, competent simple
baselines, matched context, explicit obligation denominators, causal ablations,
concurrent revisions, downgrade propagation, complete costs, reproduction, and
transfer across domains, models, evaluators, institutions, and consumers.

Formal bridges would need to show that selected executable specifications match
their prose claims, implementations refine the models at the checked boundary,
and runtime observations preserve build and environment identity. No one bridge
would establish the whole system.

The conclusion should narrow if better reviewer training and source access
solve the same failures without persistent ledgers, or if most downstream
repair can be handled reliably through ordinary version control and release
practice.

## What This Establishes

A challengeable claim needs more than evidence nearby. It needs stable
identity, explicit obligations, qualified verification capacity, adequate
context, bounded artifacts, objections, maximum inference, an authorized
belief transition, and repair to known consumers.

Schemas, tests, benchmarks, proofs, runtime observations, sources, and human
review answer different questions. Lean proves the encoded proposition.
Proof-carrying claims bind interpretation and non-claims. Tribunals structure
challenge. Claim ledgers preserve revision without claiming truth.

The current repository shows that many of these record and lifecycle
boundaries can be stated and checked over finite authored cases. It does not
show that the joined system verifies natural claims correctly or improves
decisions.

Accepted claims and plans still need accountable work. Unit 16 turns the
architecture into typed jobs, work surfaces, and organizations while
preserving the evidence and authority constraints that made the work
admissible.
